Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your own CI/CD pipeline).  
I’ll also show how to let the helper functions generate the Dockerfile and Kubernetes manifests for you – the rest is plain shell scripting.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> *If you’re running this from a CI job, make sure the SSH key for `git@github.com` is available.*

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Create / update the Dockerfile

> **What the helper does:**  
> `create_a_docker_file` writes a minimal Dockerfile that copies the source, installs dependencies, and runs the app.  
> You can tweak the arguments if you want a different base image, maintainer, exposed port, etc.

```bash
# Call the helper (this is a conceptual call; replace with actual invocation in your environment)
functions.create_a_docker_file({
    directory_name: ".",
    base_image: "node:18-alpine",
    maintainer: "Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port: 3000,
    entrypoint: "node index.js"
})
```

> **Result:** A file named `Dockerfile` will appear in the repo root.

### 2.2 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

> **What the helper does:**  
> `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` writes a Deployment + Service pair.  
> Adjust the parameters to match your image registry/tag, replica count, etc.

```bash
functions.create_kubernetes_yaml_file({
    directory_name: ".",
    deployment_name: "nodejs-welcome",
    image_name: "your-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas: 3,
    port: 3000,
    service_type: "ClusterIP"
})
```

> **Result:** A file named `k8s.yaml` (or similar) will be written.

### 2.3 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a new file at `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push NodeJS App

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Optional: set up Docker Buildx
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or your registry)
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the image
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: ./Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: your-registry/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      # Optionally deploy to K8s (requires kubeconfig secret)
      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
        env:
          KUBE_CONFIG_DATA: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}   # Base64‑encoded kubeconfig
        run: |
          echo "$KUBE_CONFIG_DATA" | base64 --decode > ~/.kube/config
          kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

> **Secrets needed:**
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` & `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` (or equivalent for your registry)
> * `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` (Base64‑encoded kubeconfig if you want automatic deployment)

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> If you’re running this inside a CI job, the push will trigger the workflow you just added.

---

### Quick sanity check

After the push completes, verify:

1. **GitHub Actions tab** shows a successful “Build & Push” run.
2. In your cluster, run `kubectl get deployments,svc` to see the new resources.

That’s it! 🎉
